label: first home
hook: Building your first home? Here’s what actually happens, in order.
sub: Land contract, build contract, the wait, the progress payments. The order matters more than people think.

label: first home
title: Contract order comes first
body: Whether you sign land and build together or land first changes which low-deposit options you qualify for. We work the order out before anyone signs a block.

label: first home
title: The land contract gets reviewed
body: We won’t let a client sign a developer’s land contract without a solicitor reading it. Titling dates, sunset clauses and finance timing all live in there.

label: first home
title: Ask for a fixed price
body: Fixed-price and completion-time clauses are harder to get than they were. They are still negotiable at signing. Ask every time. You lose nothing.

label: first home
title: Where a build loses time
body: Two places: land titling and the builder. Land delays cost you little, no mortgage has started. Builder delays cost rent and interest together. Put your energy there.

label: first home
title: Progress payments, step by step
body: You don’t pay on the whole loan from day one. Money goes to the builder in stages, usually interest-only, so repayments rise as the house does.

label: first home
headline: Building? Get the order right first.
body: Fifteen minutes before you sign anything saves months later.

label: first home
hook: Settlement day is boring when it goes right. Here’s how we keep it boring.
sub: What actually happens between approval and keys, and the small things that break it.

label: first home
title: Your deposit stays in trust
body: We prefer the deposit sits in the agent’s trust account until settlement. Releasing it early to the seller removes your protection if the deal falls over.

label: first home
title: Funds land before settlement
body: You don’t need every dollar in one account on application day. You need it verifiable and in Australia by settlement, with the transfers timed and documented.

label: first home
title: We read the loan documents
body: The moment the deal goes unconditional we check the lender’s documents against what was approved. Interest-only periods and offsets have a habit of going missing in between.

label: first home
title: Nothing new on credit
body: Between approval and settlement, no new card, lease or car loan. A fresh commitment can shrink the capacity you were approved on and reopen a finished file.

label: first home
title: If the date moves
body: Ask once, for the full penalty-free window the contract allows, and check what the delay does to the people on the other side before you ask.

label: first home
headline: Settlement should be the dull bit.
body: Tell us your contract dates and we’ll map the rest.

label: how we work
hook: You’ve got the keys. Our job starts again.
sub: What actually happens after settlement: reviews, the offset habit, the car, the equity check.

label: how we work
title: Settlement is the start
body: We run six touchpoints a year after settlement, including rate reviews at six and twelve months and an equity check. That’s the relationship, not the paperwork.

label: how we work
title: Pay lands in the offset
body: Change your payroll account to the offset and spend from there. The balance grows by default and interest falls every month without extra discipline.

label: how we work
title: Year one is the hardest
body: A mortgage feels biggest on day one. In our experience it gets easier to carry as time goes on. Plan your buffer for the first two years.

label: how we work
title: The car conversation
body: Most people who buy a home buy a car within six months. We’d rather talk about how you’d fund it now than after it has blown the budget.

label: how we work
title: The equity check
body: Once the home has grown, equity sitting in it has done its job once. The review asks whether it should be doing a second one.

label: how we work
headline: Keys in hand? Book the first review.
body: Six months after settlement is when the first check happens.

label: first home
hook: Mum and Dad going guarantor? Here’s what they actually sign.
sub: What a parental guarantor does, what it doesn’t fix, and the appointment nobody books early enough.

label: first home
title: What it actually solves
body: A strong income with little savings is very financeable when a parent offers their property as security. The loan can cover price and costs. The question becomes servicing.

label: first home
title: What it doesn’t fix
body: A guarantor fixes a deposit problem, not a repayment problem. If the shortfall is servicing, the fix is lower monthly commitments, not Mum and Dad.

label: first home
title: Their house is tied up
body: The parents’ home is committed for several years. If they sell before the security is released, a cash contribution is usually required. The whole family agrees the timeline.

label: first home
title: The legal advice appointment
body: Guarantors need a certificate of independent legal advice. A JP can’t sign it, only a solicitor can. We book it the day loan documents are issued.

label: first home
title: Guarantor, not co-borrower
body: A parent near retirement on the loan itself is help for a few years, not thirty, because lenders assess their income to retirement. Security alone often achieves more.

label: first home
headline: Helping a child into a home?
body: Bring the parents to the first chat. It’s a family decision.

label: refinancing
hook: What actually happens when you ask us to refinance. Sometimes we say don’t.
sub: Valuation first, paperwork second, and a few honest reasons to leave a good loan alone.

label: refinancing
title: Sometimes the answer is no
body: We won’t move a loan just to move it. If you already have a good rate and we can’t add a real structural benefit, we’d rather leave it alone.

label: refinancing
title: Valuation before payslips
body: Before we ask for a single document we order valuations, because the property value decides whether a refinance is even worth doing.

label: refinancing
title: One valuation is one opinion
body: The spread between lenders’ valuations can be the difference between a yes and a no. We run several before committing anywhere.

label: refinancing
title: Repricing can beat moving
body: If a valuation lands you close to the next pricing tier, a modest lump sum and a reprice with your current lender can beat discharging. Same offsets, no exit fees.

label: refinancing
title: Moving is one form
body: Switching banks is redirecting your salary into the new offset. Bills can stay where they are. And the new loan settles slightly above the payout on purpose; the surplus lands in your offset.

label: refinancing
headline: Not sure your loan needs moving?
body: Ask us. The honest answer might be leave it.

label: business owners
hook: Funding your business from your home’s equity. What actually happens.
sub: The cheapest money, the house question, the separate pocket, and the paperwork your accountant will want.

label: business owners
title: Why it’s the cheapest money
body: Credit secured by residential property is usually the cheapest funding a business can get, compared with an unsecured line or overdraft. That’s why the question comes up.

label: business owners
title: Is the house in?
body: We start unsecured or with the smallest security a lender accepts. If property has to come in, an investment property goes before the family home. Your call, and we respect it.

label: business owners
title: A pocket, not a top-up
body: Business funds sit in their own interest-only split beside the home loan. The pocket carries its own purpose; the home loan keeps getting paid down untouched.

label: business owners
title: Draw from the offset
body: Funds are drawn into an offset, never transacted through redraw. The money costs nothing until used and the loan stays clean for your accountant.

label: business owners
title: Paper the entity loan
body: If you borrow personally and lend to your company or trust, ask your accountant whether a formal loan agreement is needed before the funds move. Usually yes.

label: business owners
headline: Business needs cash? Start with the structure.
body: One conversation with your broker and accountant before the bank.

label: first home
hook: Before you sign a land or off-the-plan contract, five checks.
sub: The developer’s contract is written for the developer. Here’s what we look for before you sign.

label: first home
title: A lawyer has read it
body: We don’t let a client sign a developer’s contract without a solicitor reviewing it first. If you don’t have one, we refer one.

label: first home
title: The sunset clause
body: Developers use sunset clauses to buy themselves time. Negotiate it at signing, and never sign an extension request without your solicitor and broker seeing what it does to your finance.

label: first home
title: Land plus build vs established
body: Add up land and build, then look at what finished homes nearby sell for. If the new build is well above, it has to justify the gap on quality, not newness.

label: first home
title: A finance clause
body: A lender won’t put an unusual property in writing before a valuation, and the valuation needs a signed contract. The finance clause is how you sign and still have an exit.

label: first home
title: The grant is a bonus
body: We plan settlement as if any grant might not land in time. Keep enough of your own cash to settle without it, and chase it afterwards.

label: first home
headline: Got a contract in your inbox?
body: Send it to us before you send it back.

label: money habits
hook: Before you sign the loan documents, five things to check.
sub: Approved isn’t the same as written down. Here’s what we read before the documents reach you.

label: money habits
title: Does it match the approval?
body: Repayment type, term, offset, interest-only period. The structure we fought for has a habit of going missing between approval and contract. Check every line.

label: money habits
title: Fees: the worst-case list
body: The documents list every fee the lender could ever charge, because the law says so. Most never apply. Ask which two or three you will actually pay.

label: money habits
title: Enough offset accounts
body: On a joint loan we set up one offset per partner, so each keeps their own savings visible and working against the same debt. Ask now, not after.

label: money habits
title: The longest term available
body: Write it over thirty years and pay it like twenty-five. The long term protects your capacity for the next move. Your extra repayments do the real work.

label: money habits
title: The napkin test
body: If the structure can’t be drawn on one page with arrows showing where money flows, it is too complicated to run. Ask for the drawing before you sign.

label: money habits
headline: Documents arrived and look like a phone book?
body: Send them over. We’ll walk the pages that matter.

label: first home
hook: Buying with a sibling or a mate? Settle these five things first.
sub: Two names on a title is simple. Two names on a loan, years later, is where it gets interesting.

label: first home
title: The next lender’s view
body: When one of you later wants to buy alone, some lenders count only your share of the joint loan. Others count all of it. We model both before anyone co-buys.

label: first home
title: One lives there, one invests
body: The loan can be split: an owner-occupier portion for the resident, an investment portion for the other. It takes workshopping, but it is a normal structure.

label: first home
title: Title versus loan
body: If someone is on the title but not the loan, most lenders still want them as a guarantor or co-borrower. Decide who is on what with your solicitor before you apply.

label: first home
title: Nothing moves without both
body: Any refinance or restructure against a jointly owned property needs both owners to agree. Have the conversation together before you come to us.

label: first home
title: Security isn’t servicing
body: A co-owner can sign as a security guarantor so you can borrow against the property without their income being assessed. Most people only need that.

label: first home
headline: Co-buying? Draw it up before you sign.
body: A short chat now is cheaper than a disagreement later.

label: first home
hook: Before you sign a fixed-price build contract, five things.
sub: The price you lock is the price you pay. Here’s what we check before you lock it.

label: first home
title: Lock the price early
body: Build prices move while you wait. Once the land is certain, lock a fixed-price contract and read the terms. Builders are changing them.

label: first home
title: Two more quotes anyway
body: Even if you’ve signed a preliminary agreement, send your final spec to two other builders. Differences can be large, and the quotes confirm you’re paying market rate.

label: first home
title: The builder, not the newness
body: A new home is only as new as the builder who built it. Ask for addresses of homes they finished five years ago and go and look.

label: first home
title: Compare them side by side
body: A display village puts several builders next to each other. You compare inclusions, quality and price in an afternoon, not one a weekend.

label: first home
title: Pay for the inspecting lender
body: Some lenders charge a construction fee because they send a valuer to check each stage before releasing money. We recommend that over fee-free. It’s a second set of eyes.

label: first home
headline: About to sign with a builder?
body: Send us the contract and the quote. Fifteen minutes.

label: first home
hook: Five things we check on an apartment before you offer.
sub: There’s always a reason someone is selling. These are the places we look for it.

label: first home
title: The body corporate minutes
body: Problems in apartments are often well hidden in the body corporate. Read the minutes and ask what the last three special levies were for.

label: first home
title: The block itself
body: The type we quietly like: older, smaller blocks, no lift, decent land. Ask why the fees are what they are before you fall for a view.

label: first home
title: Days on market
body: If similar apartments sold and this one has sat for months, it is telling you something: price, layout or a defect. Dig before you get excited about a bargain.

label: first home
title: Who buys it after you
body: A layout the market dislikes is cheap to buy and hard to sell. Ask who the likely buyer is in a few years and whether this suits them.

label: first home
title: Whose inspector it is
body: The agent’s recommended inspector and lawyer work in the agent’s world, not yours. The only people checking the property should be paid by you.

label: first home
headline: Found an apartment you like?
body: Send us the listing before the open. We’ll start digging.

label: investors
hook: An investment property’s true monthly cost. Five lines we check.
sub: The brochure yield is not the number. These are the lines we put in front of you before you offer.

label: investors
title: Two years, after tax
body: Before you sign, we put the monthly holding cost in front of you, before and after tax, then multiply it by two years. That total drives the decision.

label: investors
title: A fat cost line
body: Rates, insurance, water, agent fees, maintenance, modelled generously. If the property can’t live inside that budget, the problem is the property, not the budget.

label: investors
title: Little depreciation on old stock
body: An older property brings little depreciation to claim, so the after-tax cost sits close to the pre-tax number. We model it that way. Confirm with your accountant.

label: investors
title: The growth you need
body: Divide the annual out-of-pocket by the price. That is the growth the suburb has to deliver just to break even. Ask whether it ever has.

label: investors
title: The insurance line
body: Insurance is the holding cost investors most often overpay. Three quotes with matching cover every renewal; the saving often beats any rate negotiation.

label: investors
headline: Want the real monthly number on a property?
body: Send us the listing and the rent appraisal.

label: business owners
hook: Five things we check on your business before a lender does.
sub: Credit teams find these anyway. We’d rather find them first and have the answer ready.

label: business owners
title: What your bank already holds
body: A small facility can carry a general security over your whole business without you noticing. It surfaces when a new lender does due diligence and holds up settlement.

label: business owners
title: Does the chart line up?
body: Fast refinance pathways rely on the same people owning and directing every entity on the loan. Mismatches turn a quick file into exceptions.

label: business owners
title: Every director, every old venture
body: Risk teams review every entity and director in your group, including dormant companies and former partners. We prepare the one-paragraph explanation before credit asks.

label: business owners
title: Customer concentration
body: One huge customer makes your accountant happy and your banker nervous. Lenders want the contract terms, the pipeline beyond it and a second way out.

label: business owners
title: Official documents only
body: A spreadsheet or an email from your CFO is a rumour to a bank. Portal statements, signed agreements, the source document every time.

label: business owners
headline: Thinking about business finance in the next year?
body: Let’s check the file before a lender does.

label: investors
hook: Your rentals pay for themselves but not you? Five things we check.
sub: A portfolio that just survives isn’t working for you. Here’s where a review starts.

label: investors
title: What’s left each month
body: If rent almost covers repayments and you live off your wage, the portfolio is surviving, not working. The review starts with what’s left over after every repayment.

label: investors
title: Two separate questions
body: Has it done well, and can you comfortably hold it for two more years? A good buy can still be the wrong one to keep. Selling early is a fine decision.

label: investors
title: Two numbers for each property
body: The bank’s valuation and what the market would actually pay are different numbers for different jobs. We give you both, plainly.

label: investors
title: What selling does next
body: Sell one property and the lender reassesses your servicing without that rent. It may force debt you wanted to keep to be paid down. Plan the swap first.

label: investors
title: Where every split went
body: Years later the bank and your accountant will both ask what each loan split paid for. If you can’t say, neither can they. One page per split.

label: investors
headline: Portfolio feels stuck?
body: A review starts with one number: what’s left each month.

label: how we work
hook: The bank said no. That’s one bank. It isn’t the answer.
sub: The knockback that wasn’t: how income gets misread, and what a good broker argues.

label: how we work
title: One no is one policy
body: A branch saying no is one lender’s policy on one day, not a verdict on you. We see knockbacks turn into approvals once the file is packaged and taken to the right lender.

label: how we work
title: Policy is written. Appetite isn’t.
body: What a bank publishes and what its credit team is hungry for right now are different things. A lender with appetite workshops a file another would decline on the same paper.

label: how we work
title: Income that gets misread
body: Salary-packaged pay is routinely shaded or ignored. It’s real income. We present it correctly and push back with credit when it’s discounted.

label: how we work
title: Explain before they guess
body: Back pay, second payroll numbers, leave types all look unstable to an assessor with thirty seconds per page. We write a one-page income note before they form the wrong view.

label: how we work
title: Approvals are stories
body: Borderline deals get approved on the narrative. We speak to credit first, then write the submission: what happened, why it’s not a pattern, how this loan fixes it.

label: how we work
headline: Been told no?
body: Bring us the decline. We’ll tell you what it actually means.

label: investors
hook: Debt recycling, without the jargon.
sub: Turning home loan debt into investment debt, one split at a time. Here’s how it actually works.

label: investors
title: Redraw isn’t savings
body: Money in redraw has already paid down your home loan. Pulling it out for an investment muddies the purpose. The cleaner path is a separate split for investing.

label: investors
title: One pocket per purpose
body: Equity release is broken into labelled splits, one per asset, each interest-only with its own offset. Your accountant can see which dollar bought what.

label: investors
title: Set up once, draw slowly
body: The full split is set up now with the undrawn part sitting in offset. You draw what you’re comfortable with and release more later without a new application.

label: investors
title: Check before you transfer
body: Which account money leaves and lands in decides whether interest stays deductible. Confirm the path with your broker and accountant before any transfer between splits.

label: investors
title: We draw, accountant signs
body: We don’t give tax advice. We design the structure, then your accountant verifies it from a tax point of view before anything is implemented.

label: investors
headline: Curious whether this fits you?
body: A short chat, then your accountant gets the drawing.

label: investors
hook: Cash is for the offset. Debt is for the asset.
sub: Why we’d rather you borrow for the investment and keep your own money where you can reach it.

label: investors
title: The house grows either way
body: A property grows the same whether you paid cash or borrowed. So we debt-fund the asset and keep your cash deployed where it keeps working.

label: investors
title: Never swap them
body: Cash goes against your home. Borrowing goes to the investment. Paying the deposit from cash and borrowing later muddies the trail and wastes the deductible position.

label: investors
title: Day one can’t be rewound
body: Pay cash at settlement and borrow against the property two weeks later, and the interest may never be deductible. Unwinding that is hard. Decide the source first.

label: investors
title: Same saving, still reachable
body: A bigger deposit and the same money in an offset save the same interest. The deposit is locked. The offset is available any day you need it.

label: investors
title: Interest saved isn’t taxed
body: Cash in an offset saves interest rather than earning it, so there’s no interest income to declare. That’s why it usually beats a savings account for the same dollars.

label: investors
headline: About to pay cash for an investment?
body: Talk to us and your accountant first. It can’t be rewound.

label: first home
hook: Negotiate terms, not price. Five moves that cost you nothing.
sub: Certainty wins properties. Dollars just pay for them. Here’s how we shape an offer.

label: first home
title: Write the offer down
body: If the agent says the vendor won’t accept your number, put it in writing anyway. A written offer must be presented. The owner decides, not the agent.

label: first home
title: Ask what the vendor values
body: Before writing anything, ask the agent which conditions matter to the seller. Often a short settlement earns nothing and standard clauses cost nothing.

label: first home
title: Sweeten terms, not dollars
body: A settlement that suits them, a short finance clause you can actually meet, minimal special conditions. Your number competes on certainty instead of price.

label: first home
title: Your walk-away, on paper
body: Agree the maximum with your broker the day before. Write it down. Give it to whoever bids. If it runs past, you leave. There will be another one.

label: first home
title: Budget, not limit
body: Tell the agent the number you want to stick to and hold the real headroom back. Push only when something genuinely special turns up.

label: first home
headline: Found the one and about to offer?
body: Send us the listing before the number. Terms first.

label: how we work
hook: Why use a broker at all? Our honest answer, in five slides.
sub: Who pays us, why we don’t have a favourite bank, and the honest truth about forty lenders.

label: how we work
title: Paid the same, every bank
body: Every lender pays us the same, so we have no reason to steer you anywhere but the right answer. A branch sells its own product and isn’t bound to act in your interest. We are.

label: how we work
title: You don’t pay us
body: The lender pays the broker, and that doesn’t raise your rate. The same loan through us costs you the same as going direct, with someone on your side.

label: how we work
title: Ask every bank, apply once
body: A branch has to lodge an application to find out if you fit, and every lodgement touches your credit file. We talk to every lender’s credit team first and lodge once.

label: how we work
title: Forty lenders on paper
body: Most brokers who say forty lenders really work with six. We’re open about it: we know our top ten deeply, and that depth is what lets us workshop an unusual file.

label: how we work
title: The two-day text
body: If your broker takes two days to reply while you’re out inspecting, that’s your answer. The loan is the easy part. The support during the search is the job.

label: how we work
headline: Want the honest version in person?
body: Fifteen minutes. We’ll tell you who pays us too.

label: business owners
hook: What a bank will and won’t count when you own the business.
sub: Tax-smart pay and bank-smart pay are different things. Here’s how a lender reads you.

label: business owners
title: Taxed income counts
body: Drawings and untaxed distributions suit the accountant. Lenders struggle to use income that hasn’t been taxed. If you want to keep borrowing, pay yourself in a way a bank can read.

label: business owners
title: This year’s growth, sometimes
body: If last year’s return understates where the business is now, recent activity statements and interims can annualise income with the right lender. Growth doesn’t always wait a year.

label: business owners
title: Full return, not notice
body: The notice shows the final number. The return shows the deductions, super contributions and add-backs that lift assessable income. Send both.

label: business owners
title: Years on the tools count
body: One year on your own ABN plus ten as an employee in the same trade can be assessed on that continuity. Bring the old payment summaries.

label: business owners
title: Young business? Lead with you
body: A young business is the bank’s hurdle. We lead with the directors’ track record, signed contracts and the growth story, and stack funding if one bank won’t move.

label: business owners
headline: Business owner buying in the next year?
body: Bring your broker and accountant together before the next return.
